title: Budgeting

objectives.text: Build a monthly budget from take-home income and recorded expenses.
Explain why savings should be allocated before discretionary spending.
Adjust a budget when income falls or an unexpected expense appears.

explanation: A budget is a plan for next month's money, written before the month starts. Take your take-home income, subtract the expenses you cannot avoid, and decide in advance what the remainder will do. The point is not to track every rupee forever; it is to stop deciding under pressure.

RBI's financial awareness guidance is to set aside a portion of income before spending anything. A budget makes that automatic: savings is a line item, not a leftover. A commonly quoted starting split is 50% for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings and debt repayment. Treat it as a starting point to adjust, not a rule that fits every household.

Budgets break when they are unrealistic. Leave a small buffer for the expenses you did not foresee. If income drops, protect needs and minimum loan payments first, then reduce wants, and only then reduce savings. If a large one-off expense appears, spread it across the remaining months rather than borrowing for it.

examples.title: A monthly plan on ₹38,500
examples.text: Aarav's take-home pay is ₹38,500. He allocates ₹19,000 for rent, food, transport and utilities, ₹7,500 for savings, and ₹12,000 for everything else, including a ₹2,000 buffer. When the month ends with ₹1,300 unspent, that also goes to savings.

examples.title: Adjusting when income falls
examples.text: Meera's income drops to ₹28,000 for a month. She keeps rent and the loan instalment, cuts dining out and pauses one subscription, and reduces her savings transfer from ₹5,000 to ₹2,000 instead of borrowing to keep the original plan.

keyTakeaways: A budget is a written plan made before the month, not a record made after it.
Put savings in the plan before discretionary spending.
Treat 50/30/20 as a starting point, not a law.
When income falls, protect needs and loan payments before wants.

review.notes: Save-before-spend ordering is checked against RBI FAME 4th edition, Message 1. The 50/30/20 split is presented explicitly as a common guideline, not an RBI rule. Awaiting a named human reviewer.

quiz.question: What is the correct first step in building a monthly budget?
options: Start from your credit card limit
Start from last year's festival spending
quiz.explanation: A budget plans money you actually have, so it starts from take-home income and then subtracts unavoidable expenses.

quiz.question: Why does saving first work better than saving what is left?
options: Because spending expands to use whatever is available
Because banks pay a bonus for early deposits
Because savings left at month end earn no interest
quiz.explanation: If saving is a leftover, discretionary spending tends to absorb it. RBI's guidance is to set aside savings from income before spending.

quiz.question: Your income falls by ₹10,000 this month. What should you adjust first?
options: Cut wants while keeping needs and loan payments
Borrow to keep the original budget unchanged
quiz.explanation: Needs and minimum loan payments protect your basics and your credit record. Wants are the flexible part, and borrowing to preserve them adds cost.

disclaimer: General financial education, not personalised advice. A suitable budget depends on your household size, city and obligations.
